name: Vanderpoel's Violet
lede: Vanderpoel's Violet is a muted, greyed violet from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color book, and the clearest candidate for its namesake is Emily Noyes Vanderpoel, whose 1902 book *Color Problems* studied how colors advance and retire.

sections.title: A candidate, not a confirmation
sections.body:
Gage's survey of color theory illustrates a plate from Emily Noyes Vanderpoel's *Color Problems: A Practical Manual for the Lay Student of Color* (1902), on advancing and retiring colors [1]. No book we hold states outright that Ridgway's violet is named for her, so the connection stays a plausible candidate rather than a documented fact [1][2].

Ridgway catalogued the color on plate XXXVI, hue 55 double-prime, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 carries it as block 210 [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In LCH terms it measures lightness 50, chroma 24, hue 301 degrees [3]. Its nearest library neighbors are [[pearl-violet|Pearl Violet]] and [[rhythm|Rhythm]], with [[campanula-purple|Campanula Purple]] close behind, and not far from the brighter [[amethyst]] [3]. Our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, finds 13 matches, the earliest a 1496 *Adoration of the Magi* by Filippino Lippi, and the most recent a 1915 Monet water-lily canvas [4]. These are computed color matches, not pigment identifications [4].

origin.named_after: undocumented; possibly Emily Noyes Vanderpoel, author of Color Problems (1902)

questions.q: What is the title of Emily Noyes Vanderpoel's 1902 book, the leading candidate for this color's namesake?
choices: Color Problems: A Practical Manual for the Lay Student of Color

questions.q: True or false: a book we hold directly states that Vanderpoel's Violet is named for Emily Noyes Vanderpoel.

openers: Vanderpoel's Violet may be named for one of the few women color theorists of her era, though no book confirms it.

issues: Namesake is a plausible candidate (Emily Noyes Vanderpoel), not a confirmed naming.
